source.title: The Tokens Remember: When Tokenization Bypasses Knowledge Editing and Unlearning
source.authors: Manit Baser; Aditya Nawal; Dinil Mon Divakaran; M. Gurusamy

page_placements.theme: Knowledge-editing analogue: edited facts resurface under prompts or alternative tokenizations

record.file_problem: The full paper, including appendices, is present. Some tables are flattened in the supplied text, but the aggregate results and the adaptive-editing table are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether targeted editing and unlearning remain effective against alternative tokenizations, and reports substantial bypass and recovery. It also tests an adaptive counter-method and finds a robustness-locality trade-off.
record.gate_note: The paper tests tokenization-based bypasses, which are not one of versions A–E as specifically phrased. Its results are recorded with versions ["none"] and described under fits_no_version. The adaptive MEMIT experiment directly tests version F. Table III reports many separate model × technique × dataset bypass rates; the paper's stated aggregate is recorded, but individual cells are not extracted here. Detection F1 is omitted because it detects modifications rather than measuring recovery.
record.test_reason: The study runs edited or unlearned models (MEMIT, RECT, PRUNE, AlphaEdit, CoME, LTU) on five LLMs. It measures how often alternative valid tokenizations of the same prompt string recover the suppressed pre-update answer: average 38.6%, range 19–57%. This is an input-only recovery attack with no weight change, which I treat as bearing on version E (prompt-side recovery), though tokenization is not literally one of E's named attacks. The adaptive-MEMIT experiment tests a counter-method against this attack, which bears on F.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. Localized editing and unlearning do not generalize across alternative tokenizations (38.6% average bypass), and adaptive updates reduce bypass only at a large locality cost (8.6× ripple). The authors give the reconstruction gain over the best baseline as 21.7% in the abstract and 21.6% in the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates existing editing and unlearning procedures under alternative tokenizations and proposes Toketive as an attack; it is not a reproduction of the fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, or prompt-rephrasing recovery recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported bypass rate varies by model, dataset, and editing/unlearning technique. Adaptive MEMIT shows a bypass-rate versus ripple-effect trade-off as iteration count increases. The study uses deterministic greedy decoding.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla fine-tuning used as targeted unlearning cut tokenization bypass to 0.08 (vs 0.32 for MEMIT) at 5.2× the ripple effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Broader fine-tuning-based suppression resists tokenization bypass better than localized editing, at a locality cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Most tested techniques are factual knowledge editors (counterfactual replacement), not unlearning of hazardous knowledge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Localized knowledge edits do not generalize across alternative tokenizations of the same input string.

record.problems: The paper restricts its main analyses to instances where canonical tokenization answers correctly and its reconstruction analysis to edits that satisfy the stated efficacy criterion. Reported aggregate recovery and bypass results have no uncertainty estimates stated. The adaptive-editing and fine-tuning comparisons use Llama3 and 1,000 highly entangled edit-control pairs, limiting the scope of those counter-method results.
record.rows_left_out: Table III's separate bypass-rate cells for every model × technique × dataset combination are not extracted; the aggregate range and average are retained in R1. Table IV detection metrics and the Q1 convergence-prediction analyses are omitted because they measure detection/prediction rather than recovered knowledge. Detailed top-1 reconstruction and remaining Table V cells are omitted; the aggregate top-5 result is retained in R2.

untested.parts: Near-chance targeted accuracy and retained general ability are not measured. Canonical efficacy is assumed by restricting evaluation to successful edits.
No activation-direction ablation. The 'patched canonical path, residual associations' account is offered as interpretation, and the authors disclaim it as a mechanistic claim.
No paraphrase, jailbreak, other-language or in-context tests. Only tokenization variants of the identical string are tested.
Adaptive MEMIT is tested only against tokenization bypass, on Llama3 and 1,000 entangled pairs. It is not tested against fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or other prompt attacks.

missing.what: Per-technique bypass for the unlearning methods: LTU is the most vulnerable, e.g. 51.8–54.0% on World Facts and 57.1–58.9% on Real Authors. The lowest cells are around 19.7% (OLMo2 AlphaEdit MQuAKE).
Pre-edit vs post-edit old-answer rate: 70.1% before vs 43.8% after MEMIT on Llama3 Real Authors. This is the proper baseline for bypass.
Top-1 reconstruction accuracy of 60.9%, and baseline accuracies for random sampling (30.7% top-1, 36.9% top-5).

record.verdict_notes: The E linkage is a judgment call: tokenization variation is an input-side attack that leaves the visible text unchanged, but it is not one of E's named attacks. A reviewer may prefer to treat it as a separate claim. The reader's 'supports' label for F was replaced with limits_scope: the authors present adaptive MEMIT as showing a robustness-locality trade-off, not as a robust method. Evaluation is restricted to edits that succeed canonically, no uncertainty is reported, and thresholds were calibrated on Llama3/MEMIT/Known-1000.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test near-chance targeted accuracy together with retained general ability and simple attacks; it evaluates tokenization-aware attacks against edits/unlearning.
Does not test relearning from a small unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact fine-tuning set. The fine-tuning comparison is an unlearning intervention, not relearning.

No activation-direction ablation or direct test that an internal edit blocks access rather than deletes knowledge. The paper discusses residual associations on alternative tokenization paths, but does not establish this through an internal-edit test.
No paraphrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery test. Alternative valid tokenizations preserve the same input string and are not the prompt variations named by this version.
Tests adaptive MEMIT against tokenization-based bypasses, not resistance to fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or the prompt attacks named in versions B–E.

relation.reason: Its own results show whether edited or unlearned models still give the pre-update answer under input-only changes.

tranche.reason: The study uses a new input-only attack (noncanonical tokenization) on the same question: does input variation recover suppressed knowledge? Its main result supports E. It does not argue that a version is wrong or needs restating; the F locality cost is a secondary appendix result.

source_check.notes: The bypass rate is per random noncanonical tokenization (K=30), not per fact. Pre-edit convergence (70.1%) is given only for Llama3 MEMIT Real Authors (Fig 6). Only LTU and CoME are unlearning methods. Table III's largest cell appears to be 58.9 (Tulu3.1 LTU Real Authors), above the 57% the text states. Toketive reads internal activations; the random-tokenization bypass needs only raw token-ID input.

statements.correction: Average bypass 38.6% (stated range 19-57%) across 5 models, 6 techniques, 6 datasets. Fig 6 (Llama3, MEMIT, Real Authors): 70.1% of noncanonical tokenizations give the old answer before editing, 43.8% after. The study supports E and is not evidence that recovery is absent. Only LTU and CoME are unlearning methods.
statements.problem: The 'about 70%' unedited convergence comes from one case only: Llama3, MEMIT, Real Authors (Fig 6). It is not a general rate. The study is also listed under a 'challenges' label, but it shows recovery in every cell (average 38.6%). Against the 70.1% pre-edit ceiling, 43.8% after editing means most of the convergent tokenizations still recover.

statements.correction: If used: input tokenization alone changes recovery. Random noncanonical tokenizations of the same string give 38.6% average bypass (19-57%) across 5 models, 6 techniques, 6 datasets.
statements.problem: R1 is cited, but the statement text never mentions 2609.29045, so there is no claim about this study to check.

statements.correction: Adaptive MEMIT (Llama3, 1,000 highly entangled pairs): bypass 0.32 -> 0.14, 0.09, 0.04 after 2, 3, 4 iterations; ripple effect 1.0x -> 3.3x, 6.7x, 8.6x (log-prob shift on neighbouring facts).
statements.problem: R4-R9 are cited, but the text makes no claim about this study. The study's cost is a locality (ripple) effect, not the retain-MMLU, MT-Bench or utility measures the conditions name.
R4, R6, R7 and R9 are cited, but the text does not mention this study. The study fits the factor (number of adaptive iterations as robustness pressure), but the statement never says so.
